newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Tanzania gears up for post-budget import surge.
newsitem.headline: Tanzania gears up for post-budget import surge.

text.p: Tanzania is likely to experience a post-budget surge in imports following new measures by the government to cut sales tax and duty, business analysts said on Wednesday.
But they warned that the shilling could depreciate as a result of higher imports.

In his budget statement last Thursday, Finance Minister, Daniel Yona, reduced import duty from a top rate of 40 percent to 30 percent in addition to streamlining the number of tariff bands from seven to four. Yona also cut sales tax from 30 percent to 25 percent.

"I think there is some pent-up demand which will lead to an accelerated demand for imports. What you really want is the money to go into capital goods rather than consumer items," said David Tarimo, senior tax manager with international accounting firm, Coopers and Lybrand.
Domestic demand was currently constrained but there was quite a lot of investment taking place, Tarino said.
While a weaker shilling made exports more competitive, there was a danger that any sudden depreciations could fuel inflationary pressure, he said.
Foreign exchange dealers said that in the lead-up to the budget there was a slow-down in imports based on the correct assumption that taxes on imports would be reduced.
Local businessmen postponed major purchases until the new tax rates were formalised.

One senior financial analyst, who declined to be named, said local businessmen would now start to replenish inventories run down prior to the budget while others would respond to the lower costs of imported goods due to reduced duties and tax.

In the long term, the shilling could be expected to depreciate to an exchange band of 650-700 to the dollar, he said. "We know the long term trend of the Tanzanian shilling is downward so it won't surprise us in the long-term to see a 650- 700 exchange rate."
A lower value shilling is also likely due to Tanzania's big external debt of around $7.8 billion and its heavy repayment schedule.
Even with a projected boost in export income for 1997/98, exports are unlikely to fund more than half of the country's import bill, analysts said.
The central Bank of Tanzania (BoT) will be expected to play a key role in moderating demand for foreign exchange.

"Inflation will depend on how the BoT controls the amount of money in the market. It will depend on how the BoT manages monetary policy," said one analyst, adding that the bank would likely use treasury bills as an instrument to dampen inflationary pressure.

Year-to-year inflation, excluding the effects of drought, is currently trending down and running at about 13.2 percent compared to an average of 21 percent in 1996. Yona said his target was 10 percent by June, 1998.
